catalog_quote: Bokyi, in addition to other processes of word formation, uses pitch variations (tone) to determine the meaning of certain words. That is, a particular word in Bokyi can have several meanings depending on the pitch used in its realization. The pitch applies independently to each syllable of the word. ... In Oshita (2004:107), Tawo (1977:126) agrees that Bokyi is a tone language. According to him, a single word could give different meanings depending on the pitch sound applied. For example, the word 'Dibe' in Bokyi could mean 'shoe' or 'kola nut' depending on the pitch sound applied. Again the Bokyi word 'be' could mean 'we, marry, or come', depending, also, on the tone applied. Because of this, therefore, tone markers are very vital in the Bokyi language so as to avoid confusion in the use of words. ... [p. 173:] Also, it was noticed that while tone changes the meaning and word class of a word (ie in the derivation of Bokyi adverbs), stress, in English, equally changes the meaning and /or word class of English word as can be found in words such as envelope, import, convert, rebel, addict, escort, etc. which can either be a noun or verb depending on the syllable that is stressed. Tone in Bokyi and stress in English may therefore be serving a similar function; that of changing the meaning and/or the word class of a particular word in either language.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Bokyi is described as a lexical/grammatical tone language (H, M, L and falling tones illustrated; each syllable carries its own pitch; verb TAM forms distinguished by tone alone). The authors treat 'tone in Bokyi' as the counterpart of 'stress in English'; no location of word stress, and no explicit claim that Bokyi lacks stress, is given.
new_statements.exceptions: None; only tone minimal sets (e.g. bè 'come' L / bé 'marry' H / bē 'we' M; kayang HH 'small animal' / HL 'idiot' / ML 'mosquito') and tonal verb paradigms (okí 'gives', okì 'gave', ókì 'given', ōki 'does not give').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical and grammatical tone in citation forms; the papers are contrastive English-L2 pedagogy studies by a native-speaker linguist, not a phonological description. The tone-language classification is attributed to Tawo(-Asu) 1977:126, the primary grammar sketch, which was not accessible. The same wording recurs in Bisong & Onucheyo 2020 (Morphology of English and Bokyi, pp. 6, 9-10, 118), also.
new_statements.identity_note: The Bisong papers describe Bokyi as spoken in Boki LGA, Cross River State (author a native speaker; dialect not specified, examples in the standard Bokyi orthography of Bruns/Tawo-Asu, i.e. essentially the Osokom/Okundi-based written norm). Glottolog boky1238 has 14 dialect nodes; Blench (2026, per Wikipedia) treats Abu/Baswo [aboo1241] as a separate Bendi language, so statements here should not be extended to Abu.
